title: A non-targeted data processing workflow for volatile organic compound data acquired using comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography with dual channel detection
author: Byrne, Dubois, et al.
materials: The instrument configuration consisted of a Trace 1300 GC/FID and an ISQ 7000 Single Quadrupole Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). The inlet was in split mode with a split flow of 20 mL/min and a purge flow of 5 mL/min. The inlet temperature was 250 °C. The first dimension column was an Rxi-624Sil MS column (30 m × 0.25 mm ID × 1.4 µm film thickness, Restek Corporation) and the second dimension column was a Stabilwax (5 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 µm film thickness, Restek Corporation). An INSIGHT Reverse Fill/Flush Modulator (SepSolve Analytical, Peterborough, UK) was used with a modulation period of 2.5 s and flush time of 100 ms. The loop dimensions were 0.53 mm ID × 1133 mm with a loop volume of 25 µL. The bleed line dimensions were 5 m × 0.1 mm ID. Ultra high purity helium (Airgas, Radnor, PA, USA) was used as the carrier gas. The flow rate in the first dimension column was 1.00 mL/min and the auxiliary gas flow rate was 20.00 mL/min, with a calculated flow rate of 17.9 mL/min in the second dimension. The flow was split between the FID and MS at approximately 4.5:1 which was maintained constant throughout the run. The GC oven started at 60 °C, was held for one minute, increased to a final temperature of 250 °C at the rate of 5 °C/min, and held for 10 min. The total run time was 49 min.

The ion source temperature and the transfer line temperature for the qMS were both set to 280 °C. The qMS was operated in electron ionization mode with a scan range from 40 to 300 m/z. The total scan time was 0.0241 s, which resulted in an acquisition rate of 41.5 scans/s. This is the maximum acquisition rate for this instrument when using this scan range. The FID was operated with 350 mL/min ultra-zero grade air (Airgas), 40 mL/min ultra high purity nitrogen as makeup gas (Airgas), and 35 mL/min ultra high purity hydrogen (Airgas). The temperature of the FID was set at 250 °C. The scan rate of the FID was 120 Hz. Instrument control was performed using Chromeleon 7 version 7.2.9 (Thermo Scientific).

steps.title: Configure GC×GC system
steps.instruction: Set up the Trace 1300 GC/FID coupled to an ISQ 7000 single quadrupole mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) with the following hardware specifications.

substeps.instruction: Inlet split flow = 20 mL/min, purge flow = 5 mL/min; inlet temperature = 250 °C.
First‑dimension column: Rxi‑624Sil MS (30 m × 0.25 mm ID × 1.4 µm film, Restek).
Second‑dimension column: Stabilwax (5 m × 0.25 mm × 0.25 µm film, Restek).
Modulator: INSIGHT Reverse Fill/Flush (SepSolve Analytical) with modulation period 2.5 s and flush time 100 ms.
Loop: 0.53 mm ID × 1133 mm length, volume 25 µL.
Bleed line: 5 m × 0.1 mm ID.
Carrier gas: ultra‑high‑purity helium (Airgas).
First‑dimension flow = 1.00 mL/min; auxiliary gas flow = 20.00 mL/min; calculated second‑dimension flow = 17.9 mL/min.
Split between FID and MS maintained at ~4.5:1 throughout the run.

steps.title: Program oven temperature profile
steps.instruction: Enter the following temperature program into Chromeleon 7 (version 7.2.9).

substeps.instruction: Start at 60 °C, hold for 1 min.
Ramp at 5 °C/min to a final temperature of 250 °C.
Hold at 250 °C for 10 min.
Total run time = 49 min.

steps.title: Set MS detector conditions
steps.instruction: Configure the quadrupole mass spectrometer for electron‑ionization detection.

substeps.instruction: Ion source temperature = 280 °C; transfer line temperature = 280 °C.
EI mode, scan range 40–300 m/z.
Total scan time = 0.0241 s (acquisition rate 41.5 scans/s).

steps.title: Set FID detector conditions
steps.instruction: Configure the flame ionization detector with the specified gases and temperature.

substeps.instruction: Air (ultra‑zero grade) flow = 350 mL/min.
Nitrogen (ultra‑high‑purity) makeup gas = 40 mL/min.
Hydrogen (ultra‑high‑purity) flow = 35 mL/min.
FID temperature = 250 °C.
FID scan rate = 120 Hz.

steps.title: Acquire GC×GC data
steps.instruction: Run each kava headspace sample using the configured method and collect simultaneous qMS and FID data streams.

steps.title: Dynamic baseline correction (MS)
steps.instruction: Apply the dynamic baseline correction (DBC) algorithm to the qMS data using a 2‑D peak width of 0.35 s (average of 10 representative peaks across the chromatographic space).

steps.title: Generate and refine MS stencil
steps.instruction: Create auto‑generated stencil regions for peaks of interest in the qMS data, then manually adjust each region as needed.

substeps.instruction: Load the auto‑stencil file for the first sample.
Manually edit regions to delineate each peak.
Save the edited stencil.
Sequentially load the stencil onto each subsequent sample, adding new regions for peaks not previously detected.
After processing all samples, save the final stencil file for use with FID data.

steps.title: Baseline correct FID data
steps.instruction: Apply a TopHat baseline‑correction algorithm (designed for FID) to each FID chromatogram.

steps.title: Apply MS stencil to FID
steps.instruction: Overlay the finalized MS stencil onto the baseline‑corrected FID chromatograms, shifting the stencil if necessary to account for synchronization differences between the vacuum‑based MS and atmospheric‑pressure FID.

substeps.instruction: If peak positions differ, translate the stencil in the 2‑D plane until regions align with FID peaks (typically a few seconds of adjustment).
Confirm alignment visually for each sample.

steps.title: Extract peak areas and summarize
steps.instruction: Perform peak searching within the stencil regions on the FID data, integrate peak areas, and generate a summary report for each sample.

steps.title: Combine batch data
steps.instruction: Manually align the individual sample reports into a single batch spreadsheet suitable for multivariate analysis.

steps.title: Pre‑process and run PCA
steps.instruction: Normalize and scale the batch FID peak‑area matrix before performing principal component analysis.

substeps.instruction: Unit‑vector normalize each chromatogram to its highest peak.
Scale each variable to its standard deviation.
Mean‑center the data matrix.
Run PCA and generate score and loading plots.
